title: Message Delivery Semantics
summary: At-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once — what each really promises, and why idempotency is unavoidable no matter which one you pick.

slides.markdown:
Every message broker has to make a promise about what happens when a network blip or a consumer crash occurs mid-delivery — send it again and risk a duplicate, or don't and risk losing it. **Delivery semantics** is the name for that promise.

There are three flavors: at-most-once, at-least-once, and exactly-once. Only one of them is safe to build on without extra work, and it isn't the one with "exactly" in the name. This topic is about why, and what to do about it.

slides.sectionTitle: At-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once: what each really promises
slides.markdown:
**At-most-once**: the broker sends a message zero or one times — if it's lost in transit or the consumer crashes before acking, it's gone for good. No duplicates, but silent loss is possible. Fire-and-forget, UDP-style delivery is the classic example.

**At-least-once**: the broker keeps retrying until it gets an acknowledgment, so nothing is silently lost — but a message can arrive twice if the ack itself is lost after the consumer already processed it. This is what most production brokers (SQS, Kafka, RabbitMQ) default to.

**Exactly-once**: the message is delivered and processed once, no more, no less — the ideal, and the hardest to actually guarantee end to end.

slides.sectionTitle: Why exactly-once delivery is (almost) a myth over a network
slides.markdown:
The core problem: a network can't tell you whether your last message actually arrived. If a consumer processes a message and crashes before its acknowledgment reaches the broker, the broker can't distinguish "it never got there" from "it got there but the ack was lost" — so it retries, and now the message is processed twice.

This is a real distributed-systems limit, not a broker bug. Some brokers advertise "exactly-once semantics," but they achieve it by pairing at-least-once delivery with deduplication on the consumer side, not by guaranteeing a single delivery over an unreliable network.

The practical takeaway: design for at-least-once delivery, and make your processing safe to run twice.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a retry causing duplicate delivery
slides.markdown:
![Sequence diagram: a consumer processes a message and sends an ack that is lost on the network, so the broker redelivers the same message](assets/lost-ack-redelivery.svg)

The consumer did its job correctly the first time — charged the card, sent the email — but the broker never learned that, because the acknowledgment never arrived. From the broker's point of view, silence looks identical to failure, so it does the only safe thing: it resends.

That resend is not a bug. It's the direct, unavoidable consequence of at-least-once delivery over a network that can lose messages in either direction.

slides.sectionTitle: Idempotency keys: making at-least-once safe in practice
slides.markdown:
An operation is **idempotent** if running it twice has the same effect as running it once. Idempotency keys make an operation idempotent on purpose: attach a unique key to each logical request (an order ID, an event ID), and have the consumer check "have I already fully processed this key?" before doing the work.

A payment consumer that receives the same "charge $50 for order #4471" event twice, thanks to a broker retry, checks a dedupe store for order #4471 first. First time: not found, charges the card, records the key. Second time: found, skips the charge, returns the same result.

This is what turns "the broker might redeliver" from a bug into a non-issue — the safety net lives in the consumer, not in hoping the broker never retries.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: an idempotent consumer using a dedupe key
slides.markdown:
```python
def handle_payment_event(event):
    if dedupe_store.exists(event.id):
        return dedupe_store.get_result(event.id)  # already processed

    result = charge_card(event.order_id, event.amount)
    dedupe_store.set(event.id, result, ttl_days=7)
    return result
```

The dedupe check and the store write both need to be safe under concurrent retries — in practice this means an atomic "insert if not exists" on `event.id`, not a plain read-then-write, or two near-simultaneous retries can both slip past the check and both charge the card.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: delivery guarantee vs processing guarantee — they're not the same
slides.markdown:
A broker's delivery guarantee and your system's actual processing guarantee are two different promises, and conflating them is where most "exactly-once" bugs come from.

| | Delivery guarantee | Processing guarantee |
|---|---|---|
| Who owns it | The message broker | Your consumer code |
| What it promises | Whether a message reaches the consumer, and how many times | Whether the *effect* of processing happens once |
| At-least-once delivery, no idempotency | Message may arrive twice | Effect happens twice (e.g. double charge) |
| At-least-once delivery, with idempotency key | Message may arrive twice | Effect happens once |

**How to decide:** never treat the broker's delivery guarantee as the processing guarantee — build idempotency into the consumer whenever an effect (charge, write, side effect) must happen exactly once.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming the broker's "exactly-once" removes the need for idempotency
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Our broker supports exactly-once semantics, so I don't need to worry about duplicate processing."

**Why it's wrong:** "exactly-once" in most brokers means exactly-once *within that broker's own pipeline* — Kafka's exactly-once producer-to-topic guarantee, for example, doesn't extend to an external side effect like calling a payment API, which can still be invoked twice on retry.

**Correct model:** treat every consumer as if delivery is at-least-once, regardless of what the broker advertises, and make any side effect that matters (charges, writes, emails) idempotent. The broker's guarantee helps at the edges; your idempotency key is what actually protects the side effect.

slides.sectionTitle: Ordering and duplicates together: why a retry can deliver messages out of order
slides.markdown:
Delivery semantics and ordering are separate guarantees, and a retry can violate ordering even in a system that otherwise preserves it. Say a producer sends messages A, then B, for the same key. A's request times out on the network (though it actually arrived), so the producer retries A — but B, sent right after, gets through first. The consumer now sees B, then the retried A: same key, wrong order, plus a duplicate once the original A also lands.

Kafka's idempotent producer closes exactly this gap: each producer gets a sequence number per partition, and the broker rejects a retried message whose sequence number it has already accepted, preventing the duplicate. But that only protects producer-to-broker delivery — a consumer that processes messages from *two different partitions* for what is logically one entity can still see them out of order, because ordering is only guaranteed within a single partition.

The practical rule: pick a partition key that keeps every message needing relative order together (e.g. `order_id`, not a random key), and don't rely on cross-partition ordering at all.
